utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Can we have the accused brought in, please (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Are the interpreters ready? Good morning. Does everybody hear me? Does the Office of the Prosecutor hear? And the Defence? General Blaskic, do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLASKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I hear you well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Right then, can we resume? First I want to tell you that, contrary to what was announced, we will be meeting all day tomorrow. It is the 30th that we are not going to be meeting, Friday 30th. I hope everybody understands now and that there will be no misunderstandings. Mr. Cayley, you will be representing the Prosecution this morning. The floor is yours, Mr. Cayley, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Mr. President, your Honours, learned counsel. The next witness that the Prosecutor will be calling will relate to the evidence that was called in chief yesterday, the shelling of Zenica. I will not repeat what my learned colleague said yesterday about the relevant counts, they are the same as we enumerated yesterday, but I will, in accordance with the new procedure, give a brief summary of the evidence that this witness will give before the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What I am asking is to link it with the specific charges in the indictment that I have in front of me, and your questions will be focused on the indictment and once the testimony is complete, what we ask you is not to have repeated what the judges have already heard and only to specify those questions which are particularly important for the Prosecutor. That is how we will save some time and make sure that everybody hears and understands what is going on. Is this a protected witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It is, Mr. President, yes, but the witness has only required distortion of his image. He is happy to testify under his own name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What is his name?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: His name is Mladen Veseljak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The witness, Mr. President, is a judge. He is currently the president of the new cantonal court in Zenica. At the time of the shelling of Zenica, he was also a judge within the old system in Bosnia. On the day of the shelling in fact he was the duty judge. Being on duty, he was called out by the police to perform an initial investigation into the shelling of the city. That investigation he carried out. He attended the scene of the falling of the first two shells, and saw many of the dead and injured --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me. This is a criminal judge?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: He is, your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: He attended the scene of the shelling and as I stated, witnessed the dead and injured who were lying around the scene of the first two craters. He did some initial analysis of the craters, but being a man not qualified in ballistics or artillery could only make a layman's -- put together a layman's opinion on the direction of the shelling. He subsequently attended the hospital in Zenica where he had the gruesome task of identifying the dead, the wounded and trying to establish exactly the number of casualties involved. He kept the file open on this case for a number of years, even though no individual was ever brought to justice for this incident, I think he will tell you much in the hope that some day somebody would be brought to trial for those events. In that capacity, he did finally establish the number of persons who were killed and injured as a result of the shelling, which did in fact transpire to be more than the original figures of the dead and the injured on the day of the incident. He is a Bosnian Serb. He remained in Zenica for the entire period of the war. He was not relieved of his position as a judge in Zenica, and he will make a few brief comments on that particular matter. He will be putting into evidence his report, which he compiled after these events. He will confirm that the death certificates that the Prosecutor wishes to present in support of proof of death are in fact those of the persons that he identified as being killed around the time of these events and finally, he will produce a dossier of photographs which relate to these events, and there are 23 of them, I do not intend to ask him to go through every photograph, but there are one or two which I think are worthy of comment and will assist the court in coming to a determination in this matter. As I have already stated, I think my learned friend yesterday established the relevant counts within the indictment for the Zenica shelling, but after your comments earlier, Mr. President, if you wish me to repeat that, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I would like you to repeat them, please. I have got them in front of me, I would like them to be connected with what we are doing. This has become my habit that we have now, to help the judges and the assistants for any future work we will do as we discuss this case, and that anyone in the future might be able to connect things with the events and that everything stated should be very specifically related to the indictment against General Blaskic, and not to get lost in details which do not directly relate to what we are doing, even if it might initially appear that there is a connection. Do that quickly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I am obliged for your assistance, Mr. President. The evidence is relevant to count 1 of the second amended indictment, that being paragraphs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That is persecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The unlawful attack counts, which are counts 2 to 4 of the second amended indictment, and finally counts 5 to 10 of the second amended indictment, being those counts relevant to wilful killing and serious injury.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So these persecutions have to do with crimes against humanity?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The illegal attacks relate to the laws and customs of war, and counts 5 to 10 relate to the three violations against -- crimes against humanity and -- wilful killing and causing serious injury. If you do not have anything else to add, Mr. Cayley, we can now have the witness brought in. Perhaps the blinds should be drawn for a moment and then raised after the witness has come in. (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you hear me, Mr. Veseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: First you will be asked to read the declaration which the Registrar is going to give you, that is the solemn oath. MR. MLADEN VESELJAK (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. You have agreed, Mr. Veseljak, to testify at the request of the Prosecution in this trial of General Blaskic, who is the accused in this courtroom. The Prosecutor has given us a rapid summary of the essential contents of your testimony, which deals with those events which you experienced on the day that Zenica was shelled and on the following days. You will focus your testimony on the principal elements which you observed, that is those investigations or investigation which you carried out, because apparently you were a duty judge. The Prosecutor will ask you some preliminary questions in order to situate your testimony and then you will testify. You are a professional in the field of law and therefore you should know how to testify concisely and not add in details which are not important. If necessary, the Prosecutor will guide you or have you re-specify those points which appear essential for us in support of his indictment. Mr. Cayley, perhaps you would like to ask some preliminary questions in order to situate the testimony. Go ahead, please. Examined by MR. CAYLEY

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Veseljak, please excuse me for not addressing you as judge, but if I do that, there will be complete confusion in the courtroom, so I will just call you Mr. Veseljak. Your name is Mladen Veseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you are a Bosnian Serb, are you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have lived in Zenica all your life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have and still do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A little about your background. I think you completed law at the University of Sarajevo in 1976, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think from 1976 to 1992 you were legal counsel to the Mining Institute in Zenica, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the Mining Metallurgical Combine, as it was called, I engaged in various legal activities up to 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think in 1992, you were appointed a judge, a civilian judge in the military court in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was appointed in 1992 to be judge at the district military court in Zenica. So as to avoid any confusion, that court was also a civilian court, but its jurisdiction was rather specific because it tried all criminal offences under the criminal law of perpetrators who were military men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think now you are the presiding judge at the cantonal court in Zenica, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am now judge, president of the criminal chamber of the cantonal court in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You have come to testify about specific events, being those events of 19th April 1993 in Zenica. You were the duty judge at the time and I think you were requested to produce the initial criminal report on that incident.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You have provided to the Prosecutor a copy of that report which I will now provide to you and to the court. It has been translated, Mr. President, into French and English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Was this disclosed to the Defence, Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It was, Mr. President. They were provided with a copy of it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Veseljak, I am not going to ask you to read the entire report to the court, the judges have it, but what I would like you to do is tell your account of what happened on that tragic day. Certainly in our pre-trial discussions you explained it to me with great humanity and objectivity, so if you could summarise the events of that day using your report to refresh your memory if necessary, and if you can, as is customary, as I am sure you know, address your responses to the judges.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I begin now? I have in front of me a copy of this report, and I wish to state that it is indeed a copy of my report and that these are my signatures. This report, as you can see, consists of two parts; first a record on the investigation carried out immediately, that is on the very day of the event, on 19th April 1993, and on page 4, you have an official record which is a supplement to this report, and it was compiled because certain information was lacking at the time the first report was compiled, and having obtained that additional information, I compiled this annex on 12th May and these two parts constitute a single whole. I cannot now recall, but I think it was a Monday or Tuesday. I was at work as any other day and that morning, nothing unusual took place. We were engaged in our regular activities. Then about 12.00, I really cannot recall whether it was a couple of minutes before or after midday, very powerful explosions were heard, due to which all the window panes began to shake, and we all felt very scared that moment. For me personally, it was the first experience of this kind, even though earlier on in 1992 there was an airborne shelling of Zenica, but due to chance circumstances I was not in Zenica at the time, so this was the first time I experienced explosions of this kind. Everyone else was also very scared, and our initial reaction was to seek shelter in a more secure part of the building and then to try to find out by phone what was happening to our families. I mention this because our conversations with our family members informed us for the first time that a major unfortunate event had taken place. Zenica is a relatively small town and most of us live in the centre, or not far from it, in quite large buildings, high-rises, so that members of our families were watching from the windows of their apartments and they told us that in front of the department store, which was still known as "Beogradanka", people were lying on the ground, that there was panic. The reports were contradictory, but all of them showed that something probably very tragic had taken place. Maybe about half an hour passed in this way, and then the people on duty in the police station and in the security service centre in Zenica, who officially confirmed that, as they said, there were many victims and that an inquiry had to be made. In the meantime, the sirens sounded the general danger alarm, and we stopped for a moment to think whether we should go into the street at all under those circumstances. So we were escorted by police officers and I and my colleague, who was deputy of the district military prosecutor at the time, went to the spot. The distance between the court building and the place where the event took place is about 400 to 500 metres. The court building is in the same street as where the people were killed, so we went there in a police car and upon reaching the spot, we found one crater, which was the farthest from the place where people were killed, and the policeman told us that there were no victims at that spot, which was obvious, there was just material damage. We stopped just for a moment, I looked at the crater, I looked around at the surrounding windows. The window panes were shattered, the shop windows and some cars were damaged and then we went on roughly for about 100 metres and then we reached the central plateau in front of this department store, which is the very heart of the city, and looking from the direction I came from to the right is a large housing block which we call amongst ourselves as the Chinese wall. The association is obvious, because it is a very long building, with different numbers of storeys. And then in the same direction, there is a mild slope, a lawn where children's playgrounds are, swings and sandboxes and things like that. Then further on is the cinema and then again there are housing blocks and to the left is another housing block, and then all this widens to form a square. At the end of the square is a department store and again, from where I stood, to the left is the large city mosque and further to the left and behind this building, apartment building that I said stood the length of the street, is a building that we call the old Carsija, which is a commercial area with a large number of coffee bars. Therefore in this space, immediately in front of the department store, there is a raised level with two or three steps with benches where people would like to sit, so that in this part, there were six corpses. The injured were no longer there on that spot when I arrived, and everything was scattered around. There was still smoke in the air, the heavy unpleasant smell of explosive. There were many traces of blood, of varying appearance; in some cases there were pools of blood, in other cases there were just blots. There were lots of things thrown around. I must underline once again that this was for me the first experience of that kind, and my greatest problem at that moment was how to concentrate and examine things in detail. Throughout this time while we were working, one could still hear in the distance some subdued sounds of explosions, and whenever we would hear such a detonation in the distance, we would run for shelter, and the shelter was underneath the plateau and it was full of people. Under these circumstances, I decided to carry out the investigation only as much as was absolutely necessary, which means not as we would normally proceed with a detailed investigation, but just to do a global one, that is to make a record of what we saw on the spot, including certain details, or rather in the first place the craters and the appearance of the bodies that we found on the spot, and that is what we did, and as a result of that, we have these photographs as documents, made by the photographers of the security service. The local television, a photo reporter appeared from somewhere -- I must say from somewhere, because suddenly they appeared next to me -- they asked for permission to make photographs and to film the scene and I gave them that permission. After that, we asked that the services, the appropriate services be engaged to remove the remaining six bodies. At that point in time, I did not know how many people had been killed nor how many had been wounded, nor the nature of their injuries, but I was told by the police that there were far more casualties and that all of them had been driven off to the hospital by passers-by, by the police, whoever happened to be on the spot, and who had any kind of means of transport. So we headed for the hospital --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Veseljak, if I can interrupt you there, before we move to the next part of your testimony, I would like to clarify a few matters with you. At approximately what time of day do you recall hearing the explosions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was midday, I said that I was not sure whether it was a couple of minutes before or after midday, noon. Around noon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have described the location of the first craters, the first shells, the location of where the first shells fell in the city as being a civilian area; department stores, cafes, pedestrian precincts. Would that be an accurate summary of the description of that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time of day, how many people would be walking in that area? How many civilians would be sitting having coffee, chatting, passing the time of day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very many, always. Before and then and even today, at that time of day in this area you will always find large groups of people. In those days, even more than is customary, because I must remind you that those were the days when people were already out of work, when living conditions had become extremely difficult. People started selling things in the street, so this was exactly the area where people set up small tables to sell their wares. There were 40 but not less than 30 cafes. Also there is the city mosque there, so it is the time when people are there to go for prayer. Then also there is the department store and the children's playground and an enormous residential area. Therefore this is the downtown area which is always full of people. Also in the immediate vicinity, about 200 metres away, is the city open-air market, so that at any point in time there could have been 2,000 to 3,000 people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have a number of photographs which we will introduce into evidence after Mr. Veseljak has finished his testimony. They are very disturbing photographs so if I could ask you to issue a warning to the members of the public about the nature of these particular photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think that the public has heard you. Are you talking about photographs or is it a video?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: These are photographs, Mr. President. They are part of the case file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Veseljak, do you recall how many corpses you saw altogether in the centre of town that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Six.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many craters did you inspect in the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On arrival I looked at one crater very briefly, the one that was farthest removed from the place where the people were killed. Then in the immediate vicinity where the people were killed two craters, and I examined those two craters in detail. We had them photographed and then the policeman told me that there were other craters, but I did not then during that official tour go to see them. The policeman went to do that, upon my instructions, as envisaged by the law on criminal procedure. There were another three such craters. Of course I saw them later, but I did not see them just then, during the actual investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Veseljak, when a shell hits a hard flat surface, it leaves certain distinctive splash marks like a footprint, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When a shell falls on a hard surface, it leaves an imprint which has two basic characteristics. What I am now saying I knew even then; today I know that very well. First you will see the spot, the part of the imprint showing the actual point of impact, and then you will see something like a circle of damaged asphalt spreading out like a star, and this applies always to a direction which would be in the same direction if the shell were to continue its fall. Most frequently, you will see the traces of the spot where the grenade fell, so you would be able in your mind to imagine this shell while it was still whole. You will be able to imagine the angle of impact, because the imprint on the hard surface is always such as to show the sort of entry angle, and I was able to see this in this case too. There was a crater where the point of impact was very clear and this kind of semicircular fan, if you like to call it, and in view of the fact that this was asphalt, it was very conspicuous and easily visible, without any difficulty, and we have a photograph to show this as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Veseljak, we will come to the photographs in a moment, but at this particular time, did you make an estimate of the direction from whence this shell had been fired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was what interested us, so we tried to make an estimate, but truly only an estimate. I personally stood at this place which I have described as the point of impact, of course having bent down to see exactly what the angle was of the impact. Then I turned around in that direction and stood up, and I was directed to look in the direction of Bila or Vitez, or rather the extreme south west. These are my estimates of the sides of the world, but in any event it was in that direction. The deviation may be smaller or greater, but that was my assessment, and my colleagues from the police did the same, so as our estimate, this was what was entered into the record, adding also that the remains, the remnants and the shrapnel were collected and handed over to the security service with instruction that forensic studies be carried out as was normal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You indeed have lived in the municipality of Zenica all your life, so you know the geography very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there an estimate given of the calibre of the shell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we discussed that too. We found a very large fragment which was quite intact, because you could see the various layers, a fragment which clearly indicated what part of the shell it belonged to, and then the forensic technicians who were there said that it could be 150 --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could wait one moment. (Pause). Please continue, Mr. Veseljak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So by examining this fragment on the spot and imagining what it would look like if it was in one piece, they said that it could be a shell of 155 millimetre calibre, and that is what I entered in the record, but with the reservation that this was just an estimate. Later on in the course of that same day, there were different official reports of experts who said that the calibre was 122 millimetres; of course, I did not change anything in my report, because I put down only the information that I gained on the spot, everything else came subsequently, so I did not change anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One last point on this part of your testimony; in respect of the shell craters that you inspected, as far as you were aware, what was the nearest military installation to any of those craters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To those craters? There were two. If you stand in the crater itself and face the department store, to the right at about 250 metres there was a -- earlier on it was a furniture shop, and it was not really a military unit that was accommodated there, but a kind of warehouse of boots, uniforms and a couple of soldiers, and at the opposite end, at about 500 metres, is the former army club of the former JNA, where several officers of the military police were set up, and both of these two military facilities, if we can call them that, are facilities which are not high-rises, they only have the ground floor and the first floor, and both of these buildings are surrounded by very high housing blocks, so across the way from that building is a 19-storey apartment building. The other one, where the furniture store was, which was now housing a military unit, in front of it is a large, again 17- or 18-storey building and there is only a street dividing the two, so that these two facilities, if anyone wanted to hit them, it would have to be a sniper that would have to be able to pass between these apartment buildings to reach the actual military facilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I recall, Mr. Veseljak, that you were saying earlier that after you had attended the scene of the shelling, you moved on to the hospital, where you had the gruesome task of identifying the dead. If you could tell this account to me as you did in our discussions; I know these events still disturb you now, but each and every part the court would like to hear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So we came to the hospital and there was chaos in the hospital, literally chaos. People did not even want to talk to us. When I asked for a list of the injured, people actually asked me, "are you out of your mind, sir? Are you asking us for a list now, when we do not know what is going on and what to do first?". However, then we decided to split up into two groups. I went to the pathology department where the abductions room is and where the corpses were taken. I joined the court expert, the pathologist who was carrying out his expertise, and the colleagues from the police who went to the emergency ward at the Zenica Hospital, tried to get a list of names of the people who were injured and to find out who were the heavily wounded and who were those with only lighter wounds. They obtained some data there, and then this was included in my report. However, already at that point we were told that these are not final figures, because there were quite a few injured people who did not go through this usual procedure of receiving patients, because after entering the hospital they were sent immediately to the operations room or to the eye ward or wherever, depending on the nature of their wounds and the gravity of the wounds. So at that point, the reception ward did not even know what was going on, where all the people were, how they were wounded, and later, all these data were accumulated. As far as the people who were killed are concerned, that day I saw 13 corpses and I linked them to these events, 13 corpses, 12 of which were identified immediately on the basis of the documents they had on them, or with the assistance of the members of their families, who showed up in the meantime, and there was a woman who could not have been identified at that point, but already during the afternoon we realised that it was a lady named Hodzic Latifa, and her husband, I think his name is Alija, he was also killed during the same shelling. After that, we found out in the following days that there were two more people --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Veseljak, if I can interrupt you there, there was a teenage boy who was killed, was there not, who could not be identified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were disturbed in your work by a police officer. Can you just give that account to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually I tried not to say this, because this is something that hurts me terribly until the present day. That was the most difficult detail of all for me regarding this entire event and this entire day. Namely, people were being brought in from the site whichever way was possible, some people were brought in blankets, others were simply carried, some people were brought in metal tubs, whatever they had, so when I came to the pathology ward, there were a lot of people ahead of me and they wanted to get in. I gave orders then not to receive anyone. When I walked in, I realised that somebody was standing behind me, and we were standing in front of a metal tub in which there was a young boy, the young boy was lying in it, I do not know, 13 or 14 years old. I just remember a child with a serene face. Nervously I turned around and I saw a policeman in uniform standing behind me, so this was a good way of taking it out on someone else and I told him, "what do you want, man? I told you no one was allowed in here." This man told me, quite composed, "I have to be here, this is my son". I am sorry, but this is a detail I can never recount peacefully, so this was one of these details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am sorry to have asked you that question, but it was important. Going on to the final numbers of the dead and the injured, if you could explain to the court how you came to those conclusions in your report, the anomalies that arose and how they were eventually sorted out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Already that day when all of this was happening, the press, radio and television were talking about 17 people who were killed. However, at that point I knew about 13, and that made me decide to finally see what was going on. That day and the next day I did not receive information on other deaths, but then one of the wounded, I think his name is Tarik Mutapcic, also a boy, he died from the injuries sustained, he died in hospital, and that was the 14th victim. So for about ten days or so, we had an unidentified corpse, but I should note that the war was already on at that point, and there were other corpses in the pathology ward at that time. Then some of my friends from work, from the previous place I worked in, they were trying to find out what happened to a person who had allegedly disappeared that day, so they were fearful that he had been arrested or something. We checked on that, no, he was not arrested and then I remembered that we had this unidentified corpse and then I asked them that we have a look and then they recognised this relative of theirs. In the chaos I describe that day, he was brought in, his name is Veljko Dukic and he had characteristic wounds from an explosion. There was an anomaly. Among the corpses that were brought in that day, the corpse of a man with an explosive wound on his head. I think his name was Basic, Bakir, perhaps. At any rate his last name was Basic. We had thought for a certain period of time that he was the 16th victim and then I rechecked and ascertained that this was a person who had been hit by a shell but not that day, on April 10th, somewhere in the battlefield and from the 10th until 19th April, he was at the hospital in Zenica and he died precisely that day when this shelling had taken place and his body was taken to that room too and we had mistakenly believed that he was one of the victims of the shelling. That is why there is often different information on how many people were actually killed that day, 15 or 16. Definitely 15 people died on that day. The 13 whose names are in my note, then Latifa Hodzic, whose name is in the annex to this record, and these two people identified later, Dukic and Mutapcic Tarik, so that makes a total of 15.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lastly, Mr. Veseljak, the final figure for the wounded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The final figure of the wounded. To the best of my knowledge, in terms of what I found out later too, the number is 49. However, at that moment we could obtain the names of 16 heavily wounded people and 18 people with light wounds, and later people reported in. I remember the name of Ivan Loncar, his name is not on the list, whose leg was amputated that day. He is not on the list because he is one of the people who was taken to the operations room immediately without having his name recorded at the entrance to the hospital, because his life was in danger. Then Dedic Muradif, I think, who also is not on this list and the members of his family showed up later on with valid medical documents. He was treated in the hospital for several months due to heavy wounds. However, with your permission, I wish to give an explanation here. Perhaps you will ask too why we did not establish this definitely, or why I did not establish this definitely, why did we not make a definite list. Namely, the task of the duty judge was to carry out an inquest and then to make a report. After that, I was not in charge of the investigation. I simply stated what the actual situation there was. What I did subsequently were things that were derived from my assessment that certain matters had to be clarified because they are related to those records and statements that are included in the report, and this could cast a shadow of doubt on the report itself, and it actually relates to the names I spoke of a bit earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in your report, you identify a final figure I think of 34 injured, but you mentioned a figure just a moment ago of 49. Can you explain to the judges where the extra 15 come from who are not in your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People would call us subsequently, they were asking for certificates that they were wounded that day so that perhaps some day they would be entitled to certain benefits as civilian victims of the war, and then also the hospital services tried to get their records straight and I also made phone calls trying to find out what had happened, so I am giving you a figure today that I received through private channels. I did not make a recording of this because there were no grounds for that, no official records, and I simply have to correct you. In the original text, the number is not 35, it is 34, namely 18 plus 16. So I believe it is 34.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A few people who officially addressed the court have documents, Loncar, Dedic. That is also something that is objective information in terms of the court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Veseljak, I gave you earlier a set of death certificates to inspect, and if the witness could be provided with Exhibit 225/1 to 16?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These are death certificates. Here it is Mutapcic Tarik, the boy who died later, Mandukic Fikret, yes. Vukovic Dragoslav. In my report, this last name, Vukovic, is misspelt, Lukovic, it says. Namely they were copying this from the handwriting in the book of patients who were received that day. Dukic Veljko, the person who was identified later, Arandelovic Islata, yes, she and her son were killed together. Trako Nehrudin is the boy I spoke of emotionally, I apologise once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: These are death certificates, I want to be sure I understand it. That is what it is, is it not? Using one example, the first one that I have in front of me, for example, are there any indications which relate to the shelling of Zenica? I suppose the date, for example. Are there any other facts that might be related to the indictment and then does the Defence contest this document? First of all, generally speaking, these documents are presented, they are death certificates; is that correct, is it not so?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: They are death certificates, Mr. President, as you have stated. The information in these documents which tie this evidence to the indictment is really as follows. First of all, the date of death of every one of these people is 19th April, as you have already stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The cause of death is not in this document, it is in fact in a separate document which the Prosecutor does not possess. However, as the witness has already stated, he identified at the time all of the dead and he has checked his list of the dead from his eyewitness account in the mortuary to these death certificates, so that is the connection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Is there any challenge to this, Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We are not denying the fact that these death certificates are documents establishing that these people died on that day or were killed on that day. So as evidence, we take only those facts. However, it is not derived from these documents that they were killed by shelling. So we are not challenging the fact that these people passed away on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That is the heart of this discussion, thank you, Mr. Nobilo. The question which has to be asked is not to explain all the names, because we have them, but to ask the witness what relationship there is that he could make between his own observations and these death certificates, so there will be no challenges later. Go ahead please, either yourself or the witness, and afterwards we will take a 15 minute break.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, since the Defence, as you state, is challenging the fact that these people were actually killed as a result of the shelling then as you say, the witness will have to go through the certificates one by one and state how he knows that these people were the victims of shelling in Zenica. Mr. Veseljak, if you could go through the certificates one by one and confirm that these individuals were killed as a result of the shelling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Or just to summarise, could the witness confirm that each of these names matches the list of names which he had set up when he was making his observations? We do not have to go through each of the names -- we could go through it, but I do not think the Defence is going to contest every one of them. I would like to see the relationship between the list he drew up himself on the day, he was responsible for the investigation, and these death certificates. Are these the same people, that is the real question, Mr. Veseljak. Could you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. The list of names that I spoke of today is fully identical to the death certificates and I believe that it is well known that we did not have the Hong Kong 'flu that day in Zenica. Zenica is a small town where 15 people do not die every day, so these are the people whose names are here. I even knew some of these people personally, I can even identify some of the people who are in these photographs, but definitely these are the names and these are those people. Of course, the authorities of the hospital also issued appropriate certificates to each and every one of the families in order to burials take place, and also I gave orders to describe every one of the corpses, which the pathologist did, and there is no dilemma in my mind that these are the death certificates for the 15 persons who were killed in front of the department store of Beogradanka in Zenica on April 19th due to shelling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen would like to intervene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: One question. These death certificates are, I think, in Serbo-Croat, is that right? What language are the certificates in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What languages are they in? We will have a look now. You know, it is very difficult for me to distinguish between these three languages of ours. I cannot see any special words that would show that this was written in Bosnian or in Croatian. Let us say it was in Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is one of those languages, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I did not know that I was presenting you with such a difficult question. The real purpose of my intervention at this point is to seek clarification on one aspect. Is there a column in these death certificates which indicates the cause of death?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen, if I can clarify that, there is a separate document in which cause of death was recorded which the Prosecutor does not have, unfortunately. Mr. President, we have a number of photographs which we would like to go through. I do not know if you wish to take a break or if you wish to continue. It is entirely within your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to know whether there are any questions you want to ask after you show the pictures.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I will just be asking him to describe a number of the photographs to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think the best thing to do would be to take a break now, not too long, since one of our colleagues is sitting in another case at the beginning of the afternoon, so I suggest that we meet again at 11.45. (11.25 am) (A short break) (11.50 am)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will now resume the hearing. Have the accused brought in, please. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, we had stopped just at the present that there would be comments made about the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I did say that I had no further questions before the break. It is my intention to call the photographic evidence and then I have a couple of very short questions to ask him, which I do not anticipate will take more than a few minutes after the photographs have been put into evidence. If the usher could show the witness, I think this is Exhibit 226, is it, Mr. Registrar? 226/1 to 226/23?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, this goes up to 226/1 through 28.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Veseljak, this is the official file of photographs, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have looked through these photographs previously and you have identified each of them as relating to the official file?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I do not intend to show you all of the photographs, but I merely wish to establish this point so the Defence do not challenge that these are the photographs which are part of the official file. If the witness could be shown photograph number 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, photograph 6. Can I comment on it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please do, Mr. Veseljak. That is what I would like you to do in respect of each of the photographs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a photograph of the crater, the trace left by the shell when it hit and went off, and we can see on it clearly what I tried to describe this morning, that is this area here. This is the point of impact (indicates). This point gives grounds to believe -- to establish roughly the direction from which the projectile came, and these are the traces that occur after the explosion, and this is the fan-shaped -- these fan-shaped traces and we see that these traces are only on one side of the crater, whereas on the other there are none or only very few. This is the area without traces, as I said earlier on, which indicates the direction of flight, because the fragments disperse in the continued trajectory of the grenade, so to speak, in the direction of that continued flight of the shell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown photograph number 7, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Photograph number 7 is one of the two craters that were found in the immediate vicinity of the spot where the people were killed. In my report, this crater is described as the crater which was roughly, I do not remember what I put there, I think it was five metres from the hamburger kiosk, that is the first crater. It is just across the way from the square that I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President and your Honours, the next set of photographs are very disturbing, but since the matter of cause of death has been raised by the Defence, I think it will be necessary to show these photographs in public. There is a number of them. The first photograph is photograph 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, Defence counsel has not for a moment contested the assertion that these people were killed in this square. The Defence has just said that we cannot see from the document tendered the cause of death, so that as far as the Defence counsel is concerned, there is no need to show these photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You can show them as you like, but as regards your comment, I do not quite agree. Even if you do show the photographs, no relationship has been established between the identity of those people who appear in the death certificates and the faces that we will see, so I do not think that your comment is totally relevant. However, you could ask the witness to identify these things very quickly, but we have already said that the Defence is not challenging them, so do as you like, but please do it quickly and with dignity, since they are in fact difficult to look at. I am speaking to the witness: please comment on them very quickly, because they are not being challenged. Proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you please show the witness photograph number 9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a person killed, I think his name is Cedomir Arandelovic, it is the body that we have on the photographs to the right, because we can see here that the body has been moved, you can see traces of that on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let us move along quickly if there are no other comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Photograph number 10.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Emir Redzic Tara.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Photograph number 11?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of the six bodies next to the staircase, or rather the steps leading up to the plateau that I described.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Photograph 12?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Another body from that area, I do not remember the name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Photograph 13?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Another body, I do not know the name, it was in the immediate vicinity of the previous body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Photograph 14?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, another body, I do not know the name of the person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Photograph 15 and the last of this type of photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Photograph of Alija Hodzic in the middle of the street. He is the husband of Latifa Hodzic who was also killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now if we can move to photograph number 22?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the place where one of the shells hit. This was photographed by personnel in the criminal department, I was not there at the time. This whole area is known as the old Carsija and this is where all the cafes are that I have spoken of. This is a pedestrian area, it is a square.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Photograph number 25, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a photograph of the boulevard along the Bosna River, it is parallel with the Stare Case which is just behind this building and another shell fell here and there were no victims at this spot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lastly, photograph 28?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the restaurant called "Opartija", this is its open-air garden and you can see the place where another shell went off. The one we saw before is parallel to this building, it is on the other side of this boulevard. It is in the same direction, but only some 15 or 20 metres to the left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Veseljak, you were a Bosnian Serb living in Zenica throughout the war, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you maintain your position as a judge in the city of Zenica throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in fact I acquired that position during the war and retained it throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Zenica was an area that the Bosnian government maintained control of throughout the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall any organised persecution or harassment of Serbian or Croatian individuals living in the city of Zenica during the war years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was no organised persecution of Croats or Serbs in Zenica during the war. There were cases, there were even individual crimes committed, but those persons were arrested and brought to trial, the people who committed such crimes, and there were such people. I am talking about individual cases. Those such people were prosecuted, tried and sentenced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stayed in Zenica throughout the war. Were there many Serbs and Croats who left Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were many Croats and Serbs who left Zenica. However, I must say here that I think the question that I do not understand, those many people who left Zenica, is not a big problem, and in fact I think that the vast majority of people do not know themselves why they did it. I think they believed more, they had more trust in people who described the circumstances under which they were living than the circumstances themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You think they left because of propaganda?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Quite certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Veseljak. If there are no objections from my learned friends from the Defence, I would like to apply for admission into evidence of Exhibit 224, which is the report, the judge's report, together with 224A being the French translation, 224B the English translation. There are then 15 death certificates, which is Exhibit 225/1 through to 225/15. There are then 23 photographs, which are Exhibit 226/1 through to 226/23.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is it permitted according to the procedure to ask the President of the Trial Chamber for permission to add a few words?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, but I would not like to delay too much the cross-examination. Go ahead, but briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is just one sentence I wish to add. I wanted to say it before, but I was surprised by the break. The question of the link between the cause of death and the indictments which come from the death certificate records; I think that it is important to say that according to legislation be in force, according to the keeping of books, the report of the judge on the investigation is the document on the basis of which the death is recorded. Therefore it is a valid document, and this -- the records will reflect the cause of death which I have mentioned in my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. We now will ask the Defence to conduct the cross-examination. Cross-examined by MR. NOBILO

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Mr. Veseljak. As you have heard, I am Defence counsel for Mr. Blaskic, together with Mr. Hayman. I have a couple of questions for you. The report on the investigation, can you tell me, was it customary to first determine the point of departure and then the material traces and how the distance from that point of departure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is customary, yes, that is how the measurements are made and in my report I stated clearly that we did not proceed in that way because we felt unsafe because throughout that period we could hear coming from the same direction detonations in the distance; it was our first experience of that time, I decided not to act as we perhaps should have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand your reasons and I probably would have acted in the same way, but can you tell us whether this report is less suitable for reconstruction than if it was done according to the rules?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If it were important to establish whether a corpse was two metres to the left or two metres to the right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what about the shell crater?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that the photo documents are -- speak for themselves. I think you should have no problems in acquiring full insight into all the parameters, including those distances which unfortunately we did not indicate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For instance, photograph number 6 gives us an overview of the crater. Do you have a photograph which would show the area around it and could you link those two photographs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the photographs by their numbers, but when taking the photographs of the general appearance, the numbers were placed at each trace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So could you please link photograph number 6 showing the close-up of the crater with a larger photograph of the surrounding area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the arrow on photograph number 5.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me then, please, from what angle was photograph number 6 taken? Where was the photographer standing from the standpoint of photograph number 5? Could you place him in photograph number 5?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can assume, though that is not my job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you cannot now tell us in space more exactly what photograph number 6 shows, which could be used for reconstruction purposes and for forensic purposes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can in principle place it, because you can see on the photograph here -- no, not really, I am not quite sure that I could turn this photograph around and tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With exactitude?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I am afraid not, because that is evidence from my previous answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am objecting to the manner in which the cross-examination is being conducted. Mr. Nobilo is speaking over the witness and not allowing him to answer. That is nothing to do with the translation, that is just what is happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It was not a substantive objection, but rather a formal one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I accept the objection, so let us go back to photograph number 6. We are unable to place it with precision. Is there any other crater, for example on photograph number 7? Can you help us there and tell us from what position the photograph was taken and where exactly these traces would be placed in space?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My answer is the same as for the previous question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Photograph number 8, what context was it taken from, or rather it is a close-up of which photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is of photograph number 7.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How can you tell that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember its appearance, if that is sufficient. This zero should be visible somewhere on photograph 7. Unfortunately on this copy it is unclear, but this number exists, it is left of the arrow, there is a little white square with the number, but unfortunately I cannot read it from this copy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the number is not legible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not on this copy that I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from these photographs, do you have any other photographs of the craters and the general appearance of those places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you make a sketch of the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. May I add again, interrupting you with the explanation that I have already given, to make a sketch, one had to do the measurements and we did not do the measurements and therefore we did not make a sketch, because it would not have been accurate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your examination-in-chief, you said that you stood in one crater and turned around to try and make an estimate. Was it in one of these two craters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this crater here is the one I stood in. It was this crater, on photograph number 5.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you turned around, where were you facing? Could you describe it in relation to the photograph number 5, the direction from which the shell came?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was looking between these two right buildings, across the one but last to the right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So please correct me if I am wrong, that the shell must have come over these buildings and reached this spot. It must have flown over these buildings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, undoubtedly. Shells do that usually, they usually jump over, leap over certain things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will leave that to ballistic experts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The material traces that you found, the fuse and the traces and the fragments, who did you give them to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To members of the criminal police of the centre of security services.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you give them a written or oral order, orally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I instructed them to continue the necessary activities to establish the calibre, the type of projectile and the actual direction from which it came, using trigonometry. May I add, it is customary for the duty judge to go from the spot once he has made an investigation, and then he gives instructions to the other personnel, but you are familiar with the pre-criminal and actual criminal proceedings, and only then later on do we wait for criminal charges to be pressed and so on. So that is what I did, and I put that in my report. I instructed the appropriate personnel to carry out the necessary specialised studies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever get a report as to what they did according to your instructions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not, nor should I have. I should not have received any report from them, because the file, the case was closed. We closed the case and anything that would follow depended on the prosecution, and only later on the court, if the prosecution decided to prosecute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the prosecution ever submit a request for investigations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The district military prosecution, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you are aware, did the civilian or military prosecution form a file where we might find a report on an analysis of those shells?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where, according to you, could those fragments and the fuse of the shell be found; can you tell me exactly whom you entrusted those with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the Ministry of the Interior, the security centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please give me the address as well, I would be very grateful?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a square -- I forget the address.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know in small cities, instead of the address we say, "next to the church, next to the mosque, next to the police building".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the beginning of your testimony, you said that you heard the explosions while you were at work. Could you tell how many explosions you heard and within what time period, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The time between them was not significant, but all I really remembered was the big explosion; whether there were one two or three after that, I do not know any more. I apologise if I interrupted you. I know that the explosions were very powerful, everything was shaking. Later on, I realised why, because we were very close. People scattered, people panicked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you define the space of time between them? Was it less than one minute or was it five or ten or fifteen? What was the space between the shells?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With the reservation that I cannot be precise, I think it was less than a minute between the shells. That is how I experienced it, as a short space in-between.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did I understand you well? You gave instructions for the external examination for the corpses but not for abduction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether a military commission of the BH-Army would conduct an investigation as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was normal to expect that. Actually in those days, as you most certainly are aware, an order on the armed forces was in effect an order on the armed forces with a force of law which said that the armed forces were composed of the Army of BiH, the HVO and the HOS and at the time, the military police bodies were in the process of formation and the III Corps and its command had already been formed. It was only to be expected that they would too appear on the spot as people responsible for military security and I know that they did that because while I still felt, believed that it was 155 millimetre calibre, the military bodies said it was 120 millimetre calibre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you heard that the military organs announced that it was a shell of 122 millimetres; did you hear what they said regarding the source?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I probably heard, but I did not remember. That day for me was highly problematic, because two reports appeared; there was my report that was prepared for publication with my signature, and at the time I asked the press centre of the III Corps to give an identical report to all the media, and then simultaneously I heard of this other report which differed in terms of the calibre, as I have said, so in fact I intervened, because for a time my report was revised and they read out 122 and I said, "gentlemen, what I have written you read the way I have written, even with the grammatical mistakes and anyone else who issues a different report on the basis of some other investigations, let him stand by his report". I cannot claim today what the calibre was, but I put down what I was told on the spot at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, you said that all criminal offences were prosecuted that were of an individual nature; do you remember Totic and his kidnapping? Was that prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember the case, but I think it was not prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the reason. I do not know whether they were identified. I was present personally at the investigation. Of course I did not carry it out because I was not on duty, but I was present with my colleague who was on duty. He was a Bosniak and it was our assessment that due to the tension that this would normally provoke, it would be wise for all of us to stand together, a colleague who was a Croat and myself as a Serb, and I must say that -- we carried out that investigation together with Dejucevic and another person who was a judge of the HVO at the time, that we were given security by the military police of the BH-Army and the military police of the HVO, and I am aware of that event. I consider it abhorrent, because not only the four escorts of Mr. Totic were killed but a casual passer-by. We found destroyed a Ford car and there is a record made of it. What happened later, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us this was the first shelling you experienced, but was Zenica shelled before that, apart from the airborne attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it shelled after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unfortunately yes, frequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From what side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From both sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the Croats and Serbs had left, you did not know why. Have they come back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they have not come back, or rather in the majority of cases they have not come back. If you are asking me why, for two reasons. One is the reason why they left, and the other is the situation as it stands now. The situation in Bosnia unfortunately is like a vicious circle. For someone to go back to his home in Zenica, then someone else has to go back to his home in Slavonski Brod and then again someone there has to go back to his home in Knin, and so we get to the vicious circle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My colleague Hayman wanted to ask, when you said that Zenica was shelled repeatedly from "both sides", are you thinking of the sides of the world or the warring parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am referring to the sides where the positions of the HVO was and the other side, the Chetnik positions on Mount Vlasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, we have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, do you want any additional clarifications? Re-examined by MR. CAYLEY

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have a couple of clarifications to make. Mr. Veseljak, during your cross-examination you were asked by Mr. Nobilo whether or not Zenica was shelled from both HVO positions and from Serb positions; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that. I recall the question and I recall the shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you involved in the investigation of those subsequent shellings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had the ill fortune of having most of these shellings occur while I was on duty, to such an extent that my colleagues would say that they should collect some money between themselves and pay me not to be on duty, so I had the ill fortune of being on duty when most of these shellings occurred. 70 or 71 persons were killed in Zenica from shelling and I was the duty judge for 60 of these people, so in direct response to your question, yes, I was, and I carried out an inquest and made a report on these shellings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you become familiar with the direction from which these shells were being fired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I did. You know, perhaps it seems a bit unclear now, but when you are in a war and when you are in that kind of situation almost every day, whether you like it or not, you improvise with regard to certain methods and you always learn something. Something is wrong with my headphones. I would always go that way and I know one thing for sure, in any part of town, if I had a trace and if I made the experiment like the one I did in this case, sometimes I would stand more to the right and sometimes more to the left, whenever I would face the crater and when I would see the TV transmitter on Mount Zmajevac, then I would see Vlasic behind, always. Whenever I would see that transmitter -- or if I could not see it, I was born there, you know, it is a small town -- I always had Vlasic in front of me. These shells came from Vlasic, there were many of them coming from that side, they did a lot of evil, they fell in a different way. If we look at this great wall of China, as we call it, as we saw on the photograph, they would fall along parallel lines as compared to the wall, that was the direction where they fell. Also in all other cases when I personally established that these shells fell from the side where HVO positions were, then those shells would come across the hills called Gaj Volovska Glava, so that is the direction that forms a 90 degree angle, speaking in general terms, as compared to the direction from which the Vlasic shells come in. At some shellings we had such clear traces, you know. If you have a house on one side and then if the shell falls into the yard and then it falls through a linden tree and it leaves a tunnel through which it went, then there is certainly no doubt in your mind, if you look through this tunnel, so to speak, if you know where you are, you know that Busovaca is in front of you, that it is that direction. Unfortunately, a lot of that happened, and I dare say here, with great self-assurance, that I did not make such mistakes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One last question then. On 19th April 1993, where were those shells fired from, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, there was a bit of interruption in the tone, so I did not hear you well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On 19th April 1993, where were the shells that fell in Zenica fired from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know where they were fired from, but I had a look at this and they came from that direction which I believe to be Vitez Bila, that area, but where they were actually fired from, that I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now turn to my colleagues. Judge Riad?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning, Judge Veseljak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to have some decision as far as you can give me, although it might have been said before, but the first one, you said that the shells were fired from the extreme south west, if I remember rightly, the extreme south west of Zenica. What are the cities which are on the extreme south west of Zenica which can be within the range of shelling, what you mentioned as shells of 122 or 155? Do you have enough knowledge to tell us that? Cities in the south west, within the range of such shells.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you have a map perhaps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what the range is of 122 or 150 millimetre calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Unfortunately we cannot be helpful in this case, Mr. President. I have just looked, it is of no assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Even if you were to name villages, it would help Judge Riad and it would help me too. Names have been given for cities, you have spoken about directions. It seems to me that would be a useful thing. Judge Riad, do you want us to ask for a map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I think Judge Veseljak knows well his area. Can you tell us the cities, not the range, just the cities in the south west, the main cities which could be expected to fire from there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The entire area, the way I see the south west -- I am just saying that perhaps this is not quite topographical. I am trying to imagine where the north and where the south is in Zenica. Perhaps this is something a bit more to the right or a bit more to the left, topographically. On that side, this south west side, the way I see it, that is somehow the area between Busovaca and Vitez, more towards Vitez. That is the area. Vitez would, the way I see this area, would have to be totally to the west somehow. To my mind, it was somewhere around there, so on that side of the hills, there are Vitez and Busovaca, as far as I know, and Poculica and Preocica and Sivrino Selo, but these are villages, and Nadioci; I do not even know, I cannot even tell any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately do you know how far it is from Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that way, I mean across the hill, because across the hill -- let me think. There is a road and we call it the road across Vjetrenica. It goes from the centre of town, it goes up this hill and goes down to Vitez. It is about 12 or 13 kilometres long, that road. Of course, when you take the regular asphalt road around, that is about 40 kilometres, because the road meanders, so it is farther going that way. But across the hill, it is more than 10 kilometres but not more than 15 kilometres, I think. You are making me give these estimates, so I really have to be cautious.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I quite understand, that is just an estimate. Now do you think that, and still this is just left to your discretion to answer, is it a normal thing or was it a normal thing that this 155 or 122 millimetre calibre would exist in the hands of factions other than the military authorities? Was it customary in the area, or was it even recorded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what structure you are talking about. One that is not a military structure? The HVO was a military structure. I mentioned the decree with the force of a law that says that the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina are the Armija, the HVO, the HOS and the police. If you are asking that by way of a direct question, it was not unusual to me that the HVO should have weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
