utterances.text: I am not speaking of the HVO, I am speaking of undisciplined bands which would have such weapons, which do not belong to the HVO and which are not under the command of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, sir, but in your country, do such bands have Howitzers? I do not know what kind of band it could be that could have a Howitzer in their possession. So unfortunately I had the opportunity of seeing a Howitzer, so it is not the kind of weapon that you put on your shoulder and that you just carry around, it requires logistics, it requires a position. This position should be protected, guarded, camouflaged, and regrettably I even had the opportunity of seeing the projectiles, and they weighed 20 kilograms, so I could hardly imagine a band that would have a Howitzer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You gave me the answer, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Judge, you have been a military judge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, there is -- yes. Let us use this as a technical term. I was the judge of a district military court that was a civilian court. The superior court to that one was the regular court of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was not a military unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You have not said, and I appreciate this, that you are a ballistics expert.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am not a ballistics expert.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you in your career as a military judge had to deal with cases involving ballistic issues?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would some of those issues have involved questions concerning the likely trajectory of a projectile?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you are referring to a shell, I did not have such experience, but -- because we had individual criminal cases, we had many cases where we had ballistics expertise of projectiles, but from hand-hold weapons and the like. That, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That will do. I am looking at photograph number 6 which I hold up for easy identification. To repeat what you have said, there are flash marks on one side, but no flash marks on the other, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your judgement, the trajectory of this shell would have lain in a direction opposite to the flash marks; am I understanding you correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the opposite direction as compared to the rows that you see there, so from the direction that is indicated by this point of impact, so in the opposite direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Exactly, that is what I was putting to you as representing my understanding of your testimony. You said you had the misfortune to be around when shells were falling. Did you hear any of the shells coming in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is hard for me to find the right word. It was not like a whistle sound, I do not know if I am going to create difficulties for the interpreters now, but it was this kind of sound, "hoo" -- maybe I have created a lot of trouble for the interpreters' ears and everybody else's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You did very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They do not have to interpret the sound I made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I understand the difficulties of describing the sound. I only point that I did not intend to put you to that difficulty of describing the sound, but merely am asking you whether you heard the shells coming in. The answer is yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Having heard the shells come in, would you have been in a position to say whether the shells came in from a direction which matched your analysis of photograph 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that sound made me think, when I heard the explosion, because these are very short distances. That sound made me think whether this had happened at the place where I lived, so I called my wife to ask whether everyone was alive. You know there is always an approximation. People cannot always be quite precise. Sometimes if a military aircraft would fly by you, I do not know if you ever personally had that opportunity of hearing that, you are not always quite sure, judging by the sound, whether you would look in the right place where the military aircraft had flown. Perhaps you can be a bit deceived by the sound, but generally speaking it was from that side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you deceived on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My last question to you is: this question concerns the likely sources from which the shells came. Do I understand your testimony correctly to mean this, that the HVO held positions in the likely areas of origin of these shells?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so. The HVO did hold positions in that area, I knew it then and later on, it so happened that I made sure that this was so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Judge, I thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: One or two clarifications I would like to ask before you finish with your testimony. You were the duty judge, that is what you said. Therefore you conducted an investigation which one could call a quick one, cursory; we agree about that, do we not? They were observations that you were making, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was an investigation which in some countries would be given to the police to do, what in France is called the "police judicière", and which would transmit the results of its investigation to the prosecution and with or without an investigating magistrate, so my question is the following; your investigation, which seems to have been supplemented by another detailed one, could one say that the -- did you know about the other investigation? Did you read it, did you receive it, did you supply it or provide it to the prosecutor? Did it give rise to any prosecutions? Could you clarify that for the Tribunal, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not receive any further reports and I did not expect them either, because in my country, the procedure according to law is quite the opposite. We sincerely hope that among other donations the international community is going to donate a criminal procedure like the one you have in your country. In our country, it is the other way around. Everything is done by the investigative judge. He carries out the inquest and the investigation. The police can do it on their own if so authorised by the investigative judge, or if death is not a consequence or great material damage et cetera, so the judge has to come to the scene, and I did that. Furthermore, whatever happened afterwards is a matter which I deemed to belong in the province of work of the military police; that is to say where the weapons were. We were in the beginning of the war then and what I was supposed to do is record these events for the future, not to open a criminal investigation, no, because my court did not have the possibility then of carrying out that kind of investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not have the means or there was -- it was not judicially allowed or it was not part of the hierarchy? Under ordinary circumstances, would you have opened up an investigation and given it to another judge? I am trying to understand the mechanism, the apparatus there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To understand the apparatus? Well, in order to carry out that investigation, we would have to go to Vitez, or somewhere around Vitez, which was absolutely impossible. We were in an ugly and unnecessary war, but we were divided by a terrible wall between us, so there was no chance, even if we wanted to do that, to go there and to carry out the necessary investigation; no, it was absolutely impossible, inconceivable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you would agree when I say that you did not have total freedom in which you could operate your investigation and which would allow you to determine the causes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not total, we did not have any at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to turn to the Prosecutor. During your investigation, were you able to get any supplementary information about this investigation that your witness carried out? Could you tell us that, Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We have no further official investigation in respect of the civilian authorities, Mr. President, but we do have a military investigation. That was carried out by members of the Bosnian army, and we will be calling testimony to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You have some then?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We do, your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. As regards the prosecutions, judge, you referred to judicial prosecution. Could you explain what you meant by that? Who was carrying out the prosecution, for what crime, for what violations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I tried only in principle to explain what the criminal procedure was, according to the laws that we are applying in our country, so I said the following: when an event occurs which has certain consequences, then an inquest is carried out. Since I was the duty judge, who is not an investigative judge -- please bear in mind this distinction all the time, I am not an investigative judge. I am a judge who was on duty during one period of time during a given week. So I make that kind of report and one copy of such a report is sent to the prosecutor concerned, in this case the district military prosecutor, and also one copy to the police who assisted me in the inquest; in this case it was the centre of security. In this way, I conclude my file, I close that file. If the police believes that criminal charges should be brought, they do that, and they bring criminal charges to the court and then these charges can be rejected or accepted, and in that case, they file a motion to that effect, to start an investigation, and this goes before an investigative judge who is in charge of handling such matters. This judge also has two possibilities; one is to agree with this motion, that is to start an investigation, or to oppose this. In that case, the definite decision at that court level, of course, is reached by a professional chamber. Only after that procedure is an indictment brought forth, given to the parties involved and then I start with my role, then the trial starts et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this case, was there an investigating magistrate who had been designated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, in our court, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you would agree with me when I say that at one point, this matter was not considered sufficiently serious for there to be an investigating magistrate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not considered that there were any grounds or any possibility of doing anything about that case or any other case while the war was still on, simply to record everything that had happened, and then there was this higher court in Zenica, a "civilian court" where this was all processed in terms of criminal charges brought against certain persons for the crime of genocide et cetera. It is only then that the whole matter was processed, and then the mosaic fell into place, but not within this court on which I was then and which is no longer in existence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In general, would you say that this matter was not very properly treated judicially speaking, or would you prefer not to answer my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We would have to agree on the criteria.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The criteria; these are acts which caused the death of 18 people, 49 very serious injuries, which completely destroyed the existence of hundreds of people. It was not just a simple automobile accident. It would seem to me in serious cases there is investigating magistrate, here that did not happen, that is what I mean. It seems to me that in principle, at least in principle, because you are the witness, I am asking the question whether you consider that things were properly dealt with legally speaking, given the circumstances of the war. That is my only, in fact my final question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was done within the realm of the possible, and allow me to speak to you as to a colleague now. If I were presiding over a trial chamber where I only needed the name of the person who fired the trigger, on the basis of what was done, there would not be the smallest doubt in my mind as to whether he was guilty or not. I would only need the name of the person who drew the trigger. So we did not do -- rather let us put it this way. We did whatever we could possibly do at that time, and everything that made sense at that time. Mr. President, we were in a town then in which we did not have electricity, water, heating or food. Mr. President, for six months I had only one meal per day, and at the official cafeteria at that. It is under such circumstances that we carried out inquests, under such conditions we tried to document the traces. Colour film, Mr. President, belonged to Andersen's fairy tale to us. We could not take off paraffin gloves because we did not have any paraffin. Our doctors could not carry out operations, could not do surgery, because they did not have anaesthetics. They would say two aspirins or something, somebody who would bring it from his home, so gentlemen, those are the conditions under which we carried out these inquests and we knew in advance that at that point we could not go any further. But we also knew that there would have to be an end brought to evil and that someone would have to be held responsible for that and we wanted to leave behind us whatever we could, and that is what we left behind us. I am proud of having been there, that is my feeling today and as a lawyer, as a professional, I am not ashamed either before you, our esteemed colleagues, Mr. Nobilo or anyone, that academic questions can be put to me today, that academically objections can be raised in terms of what I did and what my court did. The only thing I wish, gentlemen, is that you never never live to fully understand what I told you about today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to tell you that the Tribunal is very sensitive to what you have just said. If I took the liberty of asking you this question, it is because you are a professional in the field of law, and as a professional, we must establish the charges, we have to prove the charges against an accused present here in this courtroom, and it is true that legitimately I asked myself the questions as my colleagues asked you legitimate questions relating to the direction of the projectiles, but this does not take away anything from what you said. It is very difficult, of course, to understand from what direction the shells were coming, but while rendering homage to you about what you said, I wanted to know whether there were any other elements of the investigations which might corroborate what you did and said. As regards the rest, my good friend, I believe that your testimony is something which has -- to which we are very sensitive. We understand that you did what you were able to do, as the International Tribunal does everything it can. I think this testimony can now be concluded, it is now 1.00. The Tribunal thanks you, sir, I believe that we will resume tomorrow at 10.00. Will we finish tomorrow, Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President. (1.00 pm)

procedural_notes.text: (Hearing adjourned until 10.00 am the following day)
